translation:
A small book on the medicinal herbs of the Indians, composed by a certain Indian physician of the College of the Holy Cross, trained not by book learning but by experience alone. In the year of the Lord our Savior 1552.

To the most illustrious lord Francisco de Mendoza, son of the most distinguished viceroy of this land of the Indies, don Antonio de Mendoza, Martinus de la Cruz, his unworthy servant, wishes him the greatest health and prosperity.

From the library of Diego Cortavila.

Since in you, most magnificent lord, shine all the adornments and ornaments of virtue and the gifts of goodness that any mortal could desire, I do not know, truly, which of your qualities I should praise above all others. I cannot indeed find words worthy to depict your distinguished love, nor words with which to give thanks for your great beneficence. For your father — most Christian and devout — from whom, though I try with pious words, I cannot adequately express how greatly he has benefited me above all others: for whatever I am, whatever I possess, and whatever name I have, I owe to him. Nothing equal, nothing worthy can I find

possim mercenati meo: sed referre minime. Quam ob rem

sed meminexis, nos miselos pauperculos Indos omnibus mor

visita parvitas: & tenuitas maretur. Nunc igitur hunc
libellum, quem tu nomin Vir magnificentissime omnium
debeo nuncupare, precor ut eo animo de manu servuli
tui suscipias quo offertur, aut quod non mirabor eicias
quo merethr. Vale. Tlatilulci. Anno dni senatoris. 1552.

Tue excellentie servus
addictissimus.
translation:
I am able to honor your beneficence. I can indeed give the greatest thanks to my patron, but I am far from being able to repay them. For this reason I offer, dedicate, and consecrate myself entirely, as much as I am, as your servant. And not to him alone, but also to you, my most illustrious lord, as the most earnest sign and testimony of singular affection. For I suspect that you have sought this little book of herbs and medicines so eagerly for no other reason than to commend the Indians — though undeserving — to the Sacred Imperial Catholic Royal Majesty. Would that the Indians had made a book worthy of the king's sight, for this one is altogether most unworthy to come before the presence of so great a majesty. But you will remember that we wretched, poor Indians are inferior to all mortal men, and therefore our smallness and slenderness, visited upon us by nature, is to be wondered at. Now therefore this little book, which by your name, most magnificent of all men, I am bound to dedicate, I beg you to receive from the hand of your little servant in the same spirit in which it is offered, or, what would not surprise me, to cast it aside as it deserves. Farewell. Tlatilulco. In the year of the Lord 1552.

Your Excellency's servant,
most devoted.

translation:
7

Xiuhhecapalli . Yztac ocoxochitl . Temaxtli .

Treatment of the Head.

The shrubs xiuhhecapalli, yztac ocoxochitl, temaxtli, and the precious stones tellahuitl and yztactlalli, together with eztli and temamatlakin, mixed together in cold water, calm the heat of the head, and in warm water they cool it likewise. They are to be applied three times a day — in the morning, at midday, and in the evening — and the feet and neck are to be bound with a nerve or sinew of the throat and neck. The one suffering in the head shall eat onions in honey, shall not sit in the sun, shall not work, and shall not enter the baths.

translation:
quauhtlaxoxocoyolin

Dandruff or Alopecia

Wash the head afflicted with dandruff thoroughly with heated lye. Then a juice well pressed and strained from wild salad herbs, ground up, is to be poured over bald patches; once this has dried, the bile of a dog, fox, mole, hawk, swallow, merganser, quail, and of the white gicmilotl, mixed with wine dregs or ammi seed of Indian wine, is to be smeared on the head affected by alopecia. As a drink for the alopecia patient, let him take Indian wine warmed in unheated honey. Before the meal he should take great care not to fall asleep; and after the meal let him not go anywhere, nor walk about or run, nor exert himself.

translation:
...with dew or clear ground water instilled will bring relief.
One suffering from eye disease should abstain greatly from lust, from the heat of the sun, smoke, and wind; and in food he should not take chilmolti as a condiment, nor eat hot food. He should wear a red crystal near the neck — he will not see white but black.
Sulfur is wonderfully beneficial for diseased eyes: for this reason it will be bound to the arm, and if the eyes are so diseased that they seem nearly used up, take a pearl, a pumice-colored crystal, a reddish oyster shell, the small stone found in the little bird called molototoll, the stone called tlahcalnakin, and the stone found in the crop of the Indian dove — grind these in the blood of a goose, woman's milk, and spring water, and having prepared it thus, instill it over the affected eyes.
But when something more deadly occurs, and from it the eyes begin to putrefy, there should be instilled into them a concentrated liquor made with a pod-shell, salt, and flour with spring water. If however this affliction has arisen from cold, it is remedied if a pumice-colored crystal is ground in the juice of the indigo plant and the liquid is instilled into the eyes.

Sanguis oculos occupans.

Hoc vitium tollitur si oculi cinere suffusi humano oleo puluerato conspergantur. Eodem quoq; remedio oculoru argemala albugines, vitiate oculorum inquisitie, recentis ani tritum putamen cum eiusdem intello & cum cinere colate in acerba vel acri aqua octo dies positum & postea instillatum, est valde efficax.
translation:
Blood occupying the eyes.

This condition is cured if the eyes, suffused with blood, are sprinkled with powdered human ash and oil. By the same remedy also, argemata and white spots of the eyes, and diseased conditions of the eyes: the freshly ground shell of a walnut, together with its inner membrane, strained with ash in sharp or bitter water, left for eight days and thereafter instilled drop by drop, is very effective.

Toothache

Loose and rotting teeth must first be pricked with a dead man's tooth. Then the root of the shrub called Teonochili is ground up and mixed together with reed horn, with the precious stones called itzquetzalitzth, red tapachtli, and a small amount of flour or meal, and should be warmed with salt. Gout

A person suffering from gout may be cured in the following manner. The branches of pilzintecouhxochitl, fronds of cypress and laurel are rubbed into a scabby ant-hill, and those who pass through it are sprinkled with a bath made from these. Furthermore, the shrubs of quappoquietl, the leaves and bark of ayahqualuill, the leaves of qualmiqui, halqqqal, and the flowers of tepechian of this herb; a white small stone or pumice, the herb called yhcrinpahtli, pine, and a shell are ground together with the warmth of a hare. Little foxes, rabbits, small serpents, hecacohuatl, lizards are also used, along with a pearl, an emerald, and cztetl in water. If the foot is afflicted by excessive heat, let it be bathed in cold juice; but if it grows too cold, it must be warmed up. To the above-mentioned things add thin slices of saffron color. You shall burn the flesh of a small fox and its fat as well.

The appearance of a feverish person changes in many ways: sometimes the face turns red, sometimes dark, sometimes pale. The person also spits blood, vomits, tosses and turns the body this way and that, sees poorly. If the urine turns white, the patient is immediately in danger, and medicine will be prepared too late. translation:
Colomecatl.

Hemorrhoids.

Against hemorrhoids, the stem of the herb Colomecatl is very effective. For when it is ground with honey in warm water, if the juice is drunk, it draws out the bile. Second, teohonatli, the herb that grows over pestilence, is prepared by decoction, so that that juice, which abounds in milk, may flow out. It is to be taken with cotton and dried a little in the sun, and drunk moderately, by which pale bile is drawn out. Within a few days the medicine heals what it would otherwise dissolve. Furthermore, a medicine is made from the herbs quauh yzeçochitl and a sun-dried bark, bitter when warmed. This indeed draws out the purulence and cleanses the belly of man. Before lunch, let him eat a weasel that has been killed and notably prepared, together with the heart of a dragon.

Condyloma.

The bark of oak, the bark of huiiquahuill, and the barks of apollaxipetnalli and tlacoxiloxochitl are to be ground together. A preparation is made by drying in the sun, mixing things that need to be warmed, or preferably cooked. A cloth is soaked in honey, with which the condyloma is touched and rubbed. If this affliction is in the nostrils or near the anus, warm water should be poured over it, and it should also be washed with the juice from the bark of teo amotl, to which honey is added. Having made this juice into a softening medicine, the part afflicted with condyloma should be bathed with it as frequently as possible.

Excessive heat.

The body burning with fever is cooled by the roots of these plants, namely: xaliomati, tlacacamōhlli, ieconstaquilit, the stone smallotēll, estēll, tlalcalmagm, red earth, white earth, the small stones that form in the gizzard of the rooster, and noch totōtl — all of these are to be placed in water. translation:
Cuecuechpahlli

A Recurring Illness.

One who falls ill again should, before a meal, drink the juice pressed from something very similar to teohamatl milk, which causes vomiting. On the third or fourth day, let him drink a preparation made from tonaliu, from the stem of xiuh herb, and itatlanquaye, and also from flanexti herb, likewise using the stem, steeped in warm water. Third, let him drink from cuecuechpahlli, the stem ground in our wine. Into the potion he is to drink, let there be added ingredients for a bath, from which he will emerge, having sweated out the bitter liquid of the teohamatl bark. The alder serves twice as a purging enema. First, from the juice of the root of ohuaxoco, placed in water in a tub, so that he may absorb something of it. This juice indeed expels pus from the kidneys. As a final remedy, a few doses on successive days, a preparation made from the ground herb in wine sufficient to intoxicate. As for what bocomis piu yet yields: salt, black pepper, and pepper of a pale color.

Joint Disease.

To prepare a poultice against joint pain, take cuauhxixicatzin, tetzitzicatzin, colosxixquitl, patlahuacxitzicathi, and xuhillemayh — these are herbs — along with serpents, scorpions, and centipedes, which are ground together in water and strained. When this roughness of the skin takes hold of the body, take the bark of cherry, oak, and cypress trees; hanexcia wood, bramble; roots of the herbs tlayapaloni, tlalhaueueti, yolohua xihuitl; oak apple leaves and the herb tleltlanquaye — these are placed in water and boiled together with broth and ground squirrel egg. The affected part of the body, the one having pustular sores, is washed with the broth; afterward the prepared medicine is applied to it.

Remedy for Festering Wounds Already Infected with Worms.

When you observe that a wound is already crawling with worms, grind together the leaves of quezalmizquitl, cimati, tlalcacapol, and ueprum, also the root of tlaquilm and the bark of xilexochitl, and do this in our finest wine. text:
Quezalxahoyait. Ococol. tli. Tetzitzilm.

C mitialis morbus.

Contra morbū sacru recens exortum valebūt lapilli in ventriculis accipitris, auriculaxum huactli et galli inuct, radix quezalxahoyait, cornu cerui tus subalbum, tus albidūm, cadaueris capillus, talpæ in olla incluse caro combusta, que quidem bene terenda sunt in calfacta aqua. Succum bibet, et vomit comitialis homo. et ante hunc non fuerit inutile eum bibere succum fruticis nomine tlahllacotic, radix terenda est.

Obserua tempus, quo epilepsia venitura est. tunc enim te poris vnestigio comitialis homo erigendus est. et cartilago et latera pungenda sunt. Ingens autem fel caninum bibat, simul et caput perfundatur malagmate confecto ex que zalachayait. et tetzitzilm frondibus. et herba vel frutice acocohxihuill triuis in aqua. Vulpis et mustelle cerebrum coctum edet. Bono aut odore murium iridi in prunauo combusti, subali turis. et auis cozca quauhtli plumis sufficiendus vel suffumigandus erit.
translation:
Quezalxahoyait. Ococol. tli. Tetzitzilm.

Epilepsy [Falling Sickness].

Against the sacred disease recently arisen, the following will be effective: small stones from the stomach of a hawk, the ears of the great horned owl and a rooster, the root of quezalxahoyait, stag's horn burnt to a whitish ash, white incense, the hair of a corpse, the flesh of a mole enclosed and burned in a clay pot — all of these must be well ground together in warm water. The epileptic person shall drink the liquid and vomit. And before this, it would not be useless for him to drink the juice of a shrub called tlahllacotic; its root must be ground.

Observe the moment when a seizure is about to come on. For at that very instant the epileptic must be made to stand upright, and his cartilage and sides must be pricked. Let him then drink a large amount of dog's bile, and at the same time let his head be bathed with a poultice prepared from zalachayait and the leaves of tetzitzilm and the herb or shrub acocohxihuill, ground in water. He shall eat the cooked brain of a fox and a weasel. And he must be fumigated with the pleasant smell of burned mouse droppings on hot coals, and with white incense, and with the feathers of the eagle called cozca quauhtli.

For one who has been afflicted by a whirlwind or an evil wind,
and how he shall be cured.

The juice is boiled down, and he shall drink the decoction. For when taken, it drives out the evil air that has entered. Second, let him drink ground stones dissolved in water: red crystals, white pearls, white earth, and the leaves of the herb tlatlanquaye, which you shall boil together with bile. Anoint him with the seeds of cypress and cedar, and the leaves of the tree quauhyayauhth, and the leaves of the herb xiuhecapahtli, ground in water, with a carefully prepared liquid of bile.

53

Cacaloxochitl. Necouhxochitl

A Remedy for Fear and Faint-heartedness

One who is fearful shall take a drink prepared from the herb tonahius, which further expels misery. The herbs tlanextia xihuiti and tlahauiti, and white earth, are to be dissolved in river water or stream water; to these are added the flowers of cacaloxochitl, cacauaxochitl, and itacouhxochitl. Anoint him with a poultice, which you must make from sulfur, the blood of a tick, the color of the worm senecioyolotli, and dung, along with lamium, swallow dung ground in water, and sea foam.

One who has been terrified by lightning or thunderbolt shall be anointed with the dried leaves of the tree that was struck by lightning and with all the plants that grow near it. Furthermore, the water used to dissolve the ointment shall have a sour taste.

Contra abde velica mortes

Qui tali mente preciosa est, trite tlah tlacolic radices in cali facta aqua succum bibat et vomat. paucis post diebus flo rum yolloxochitl et cacauaxochitl et cortices et radices in aqua terantur: succumq bibat ante prandium, quo malo humor pectus occupans altissime demittatur. Tertio lapillos avium xiuhquecholtotl et tlapalototl ventium, te tlahuitl, preciosos lapides tlahcalhuam. Estell. et mar garitum conterito in aqua. Porro liquorem dimidie par tem bibet, et partem capiti subinde infindes. Hoc per acto manibus gestabit lapillum in dente huaelli muelus nocti simulet fel: nam hac gestatione et potione resipis et in mentis sanitatem restituetur. Sinciput autem un gere cervino cerebro et cahimbe plurimis totus et pos itis morqua ac humaris capillos. Collo gestabit lapil lum in dente hirundinis repertum.
translation:
Cacauaxochitl chili. Yolloxochitl chili.

Against sudden death of the mind

He who is afflicted in his precious mind: let him grind the roots of tlah tlacolic in heated water and drink the juice and vomit. A few days later, let the flowers of yolloxochitl and cacauaxochitl, along with their barks and roots, be ground in water; let him drink the juice before eating, so that the evil humor occupying the chest may be driven down deeply. Third, grind together the small stones found in the birds xiuhquecholtotl and tlapalototl, tlahuitl, the precious stones tlahcalhuam, estell, and pearl in water. He shall drink half of this liquid, and the other half shall be poured repeatedly over his head. When this is done, he shall carry in his hands a small stone found in the tooth of the huaelli, which resembles bile at night; for by this carrying and drinking he will recover and be restored to soundness of mind. Furthermore, anoint the crown of the head with deer brain and cahimbe applied abundantly all over, along with morqua and human hair. Around the neck he shall carry a small stone found in the tooth of a swallow.

This offensive odor is removed by anointing the body with a preparation of the herbs ayauhtonanxochitl, papaloquilitl, and coinbecapahili, in the juice of their crushed leaves. One may also use the juice of the leaves and flowers of otoxochitl, tonacayxochitl, totolockim, and spikenard.

Hircus or tragus of the armpit.

translation:
Quauhalac. Cihuapahtli. Quetzalahicexotl.
Hinae.

A remedy for recent childbirth

If a woman is suffering difficulty in giving birth, so that she may hold and deliver her infant with little pain, she should drink a medicine made from the bark of the quauhalac tree boiled in water, together with the herb Cihuapahtli, a small stone called zotett, and the tail of the little creature called tlaquatzin [opossum]. She should carry the herb tlanextica in her hand. Furthermore, let the feathers and bones of an eagle's wing, the tree quetzalaexotl, deer hide, the bile of a rooster and hen, the bile of a hare, and dried onions be burned together; to these add salt, the fruit called in our tongue Nochili [nopal fruit], and otli. Let these aforesaid things be warmed and the body anointed with their juice. She should eat cooked flesh seasoned with sulphur, and smaragdine stones are firmly bound to the shoulders. She may also take in sweet local wine the ground fibers of a kite's dung and the tail juice of the tlaquatzin. Also, let the stalk of xaltomali, the tail of the tlaquatzin, and the leaves of cihuapahtli be ground, and with their liquid let the womb be moistened. Likewise grind the large tail of the tlaquatzin, and with the juice of the herb cihuapahtli, administered as an enema, wash or anoint the area.

text:
Xinheloquiliti. Tlacopopoti.

Ventris puerpere lotio.

Mulieris parturi propinque venter abluendus est succo herbarum xinheloquiliti, tlacopopoti, centzontxochitl, xinpali, lanj, que teres in fontana aqua cum lapide Ezteli et teslahuitl. Hac etiam latice sepinsule abluendi sunt pedes. Si iam edendus fetus in proximo est, teritur etiam yztac huiqualnitl, malinalli, albidus lapis, albicum nitium, pinus, palma et ezteli in aqua alco quantire.
translation:
Xinheloquiliti. Tlacopopoti.

Washing of the belly of a woman in labor.

The belly of a woman near childbirth is to be washed with the juice of the herbs xinheloquiliti, tlacopopoti, centzontxochitl, xinpali, lanj, which you shall grind in spring water together with the stone ezteli and teslahuitl. With this same liquid the feet are also to be washed repeatedly. If the birth of the child is now imminent, one also grinds yztac huiqualnitl, malinalli, white stone, white nitium, pine, palm, and ezteli in water in a sufficient quantity.

text:

In vulvam autem immities tritam herbam ayonelhuatl,
aquilinum fimum, herbas acetarias, radicem quanhtlahnac & lapillum eztell quo dolore levabitur.
translation:

Against burns in infants.

Siriasis, which is a burning affliction of infants, is cured if the body is anointed with a poultice made from the well-known seed michihuathlli, ground with red ochre and grain. Blood that is pale or black is a messenger of death from the belly. Furthermore, the face growing pale, turning dark, and taking on one expression after another; and especially if words tumble out without sense, like a parrot, pouring them forth in no order.

In a woman, moreover, one special sign has been observed, namely if the buttocks, thighs, and sides are pricked as if by a very sharp thorn.

Yet against a desperate and hopeless condition, you may still instill into the eyes of the dying a medicine carefully made from precious stones — tlahcalhuahieztoll, pearl, and white pearl — ground to a pale powder in water.
